title: The Climber?: Prelude and Fugue No.4, Book I
content_blocks: This prelude slowly explores and expands the range of the piano, in ever widening fanned-out chords—a bit like a weird, slow Aaron Copland piece.  As the music reaches the widest range at the end of the prelude, the chords become more and more consonant, finally moving solely through the notes of the E-flat major scale.  This is a surprise, given the unusual and ambiguous beginning of the piece.

The last note of the prelude becomes the first note of the fugue, which enriches the E-flat major sound and moves into a sound similar to a Debussy prelude. The unusual thing about the fugue is that after a trill and then an arpeggio (reminiscent of the last section of Debussy’s prelude Voiles), the melody line splits into two, moving in parallel. Each of the three voices of this fugue split in similar ways, leading to a passage with six-note chords that evoke parts of the prelude.

This prelude and fugue, together with Nos.2 and 9, were the last added, and I never came up with a descriptive label.  I would be tempted to call this pair “The Dreamer,” but that’s the label I used for No.3.  Perhaps, in the way that the prelude climbs to higher and higher heights, and then emerges into a calmly serene fugue—perhaps by a lake, with birds and sailboats?—it could be called “The Climber”?
David Kaplan’s performance brings out the harmonic ambiguity of the Prelude and the gauzy (high altitude?) quality of the Fugue.
